analysis.investment_thesis: Exim Routes scores well on ROCE (55%) but catastrophically fails the Magic Formula on earnings yield (~3.9%) and shows zero years of positive operating cash flow — meaning the reported profits are not translating into real cash. At 37.5x P/E on a 5-year-old commodity paper trading business with INR 8 Cr net profit, the valuation is punishing for what is ultimately a thin-margin intermediary.
key_strengths: Exceptional ROCE of 55.3% — suggests capital-light model with strong pricing power in its niche
Revenue hypergrowth: 4Y CAGR of 134.5%, growing from INR 4 Cr to INR 121 Cr
Moderate promoter holding (52.4%) with meaningful FII+DII participation (13.9%) for a micro-cap
key_risks: Negative OCF every single year (0/5 positive); FY25 OCF = -5 Cr despite INR 8 Cr net profit — profit quality is highly suspect
Earnings Yield ≈ 3.9% (EBIT INR 10 Cr / EV ~INR 257 Cr) — far below the 12% Magic Formula threshold; deeply overvalued
Commodity paper trading is a low-moat, volume-driven business exposed to input price swings, credit risk, and margin compression
red_flags: FCF has been negative all 5 years; FY25 FCF = -9 Cr while net profit = +8 Cr — a ~17 Cr divergence is alarming
Business funded entirely by external financing (Financing CF +11 Cr in FY25); operations and investments are cash drains
Incorporated April 2019 — only 2 years of meaningful profit; no track record through a full business cycle
Total equity jumped from 4 Cr (FY24) to 25 Cr (FY25) via capital raise, which inflated the balance sheet and may be distorting ROCE
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Magic Formula verdict is swift: Earnings Yield of ~3.9% (EBIT ≈ INR 10 Cr ÷ EV ≈ INR 257 Cr) is less than one-third of Greenblatt's minimum attractive threshold of 12%. The only redeeming metric is ROCE of 55%, but one-half of the Magic Formula being broken means this stock simply doesn't qualify. A P/E of 37.5x on a commodity paper-trading intermediary incorporated in 2019 with INR 8 Cr of net profit embeds enormous growth expectations with no margin of safety.

The cash flow picture is the most disqualifying factor. Despite cumulative net profit turning positive in FY24-25, operating cash flow has been negative in every recorded year — including -5 Cr in FY25 against +8 Cr net profit. This gap is a hallmark of working capital-intensive trading models where receivables and inventory consume cash faster than profits are generated. The business is surviving on financing (equity raise + borrowings), not operations. Until OCF turns structurally positive and FCF follows, the reported ROIC numbers cannot be trusted as durable value creation. Greenblatt's framework explicitly requires real earnings; here, the earnings are not backed by cash.
